chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Hadid, from Abu al-Mi'za, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding two men who shared in wealth and made a profit from it, and the wealth was a debt upon them, one said to his partner: 'Give me the principal, and the profit is yours, and whatever I owe (you), you owe (me).' He said: 'There is no harm with it if it is stipulated upon him, and even if it is a condition that contradicts the Book of Allah, Exalted and Mighty, it is a return to the Book of Allah.'
And he said: 'In all animals, there is a stipulation of three days for the buyer, and he is at option during them, whether stipulated or not stipulated.'

And from a man who bought a sheep and kept it for three days then returned it, he said: 'If during those three days he drank its milk, he returns with it three Amadds, and if it did not have milk, there is nothing upon him.'
ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic legal rulings on shared debt in partnership and the return of purchased animals?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the validity of conditional clauses in partnerships, noting that even if a condition contradicts the literal text of the Quran, it remains binding unless it violates a fundamental principle. It further establishes the three-day *khiyar* (option period) for animal sales, a standard practice in Shia jurisprudence for inspecting livestock, and specifies the compensation (*dam*) required for milk consumed during this period, reflecting the practical application of contract law in early Islamic commerce.
